title: Pozole
subtitle: Mexican pork and hominy stew
excerpt: A rich, deeply flavoured Mexican stew made with slow-cooked pork, hominy (maize kernels), and a red chilli broth. It is traditionally garnished with shredded cabbage, lime, and dried oregano.
sourceNotes: Pozole is one of Mexico's oldest dishes, with pre-Columbian origins. It was eaten at Aztec ceremonies and has remained a ceremonial and celebratory food across Mexico ever since.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the broth and meat separately from the garnishes.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day. Store in the fridge and reheat gently.

content.text: Pork shoulder is the right cut for pozole. The fat and collagen melt into the broth over a long simmer and give it a rich, unctuous texture. Do not rush the cooking.

items.prepNote: use hominy (dried or tinned maize kernels) if available -- or 2 x 400g tins of chickpeas, drained

content.text: Place the pork, onion quarters, and garlic in a large pot. Cover with the chicken stock. Bring to a boil.
Skim the foam from the surface. Reduce heat and simmer for 1 hour.
Remove the pork and shred it with two forks. Set aside.
Blend the tinned tomatoes with the smoked paprika, cumin, and oregano. Pour into the broth.
Add the hominy or chickpeas to the broth. Simmer for 30 minutes.
Return the shredded pork to the pot. Simmer for 10 more minutes. Season well.
Ladle into deep bowls. Top with shredded cabbage and a squeeze of lime juice.

items.cause: Foam not skimmed at the start
items.fix: Always skim the foam in the first 10 minutes of simmering. This keeps the broth clean and clear.

items.cause: Heat too low or pork pieces too large
items.fix: Continue simmering for another 30 minutes. Pork shoulder needs time. Large pieces can take up to 2 hours.

items.cause: Not reduced enough or too much stock
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for 20 more minutes to concentrate the flavour. Season generously.

content.text: Pozole is one of Mexico's most ancient dishes. It was eaten at Aztec religious ceremonies long before European contact. Maize was sacred in Mesoamerican cultures and the hominy in pozole connects the dish to that heritage. Today it is eaten at Mexican celebrations, family gatherings, and as a restorative dish for cold evenings. Regional versions differ between red, white, and green broths.
